claim: Mechanical stimulation of a single murine osteoblast led to the release of 70 ± 24 amole ATP.
source: Mechanical stimulation of a single murine osteoblast led to the release of 70 ± 24 amole ATP, which stimulated calcium responses in neighboring cells.
evidence: The manuscript reports a specific quantitative measurement of ATP release from mechanically stimulated osteoblasts.

claim: Mechanically released ATP stimulated calcium responses in neighboring cells.
source: Mechanical stimulation of a single murine osteoblast led to the release of 70 ± 24 amole ATP, which stimulated calcium responses in neighboring cells.

claim: Interventions that promoted vesicular release reduced ATP release.

claim: Inhibitors of vesicular release potentiated ATP release.

claim: Bone loss occurs in astronauts exposed to microgravity.
source: The mechanical environment is an important determinant of bone health, as emphasized by a consistent bone loss in astronauts exposed to microgravity or in paralyzed or bedridden patients (Nagaraja and Jo, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this established observation.

claim: Osteocytes and osteoblasts are the mechanosensitive cells in the skeletal system.
source: Bone-embedded osteocytes and bone-forming osteoblasts are widely regarded as the mechanosensitive cells in the skeletal system (Weinbaum et al., 1994).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this established concept.

claim: Transient intracellular free calcium elevations are among the earliest detectable events following mechanical stimulation of osteoblasts.
source: Following mechanical stimulation of rodent and human osteoblasts, transient intracellular free calcium ([Ca2+]i) elevations and ATP release are among the earliest detectable events, which result in autocrine and paracrine purinergic (P2) receptor signaling (Robling and Turner, 2009; Romanello et al., 2001; Genetos et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this established observation.

claim: ATP release is among the earliest detectable events following mechanical stimulation of osteoblasts.
source: Following mechanical stimulation of rodent and human osteoblasts, transient intracellular free calcium ([Ca2+]i) elevations and ATP release are among the earliest detectable events, which result in autocrine and paracrine purinergic (P2) receptor signaling (Robling and Turner, 2009; Romanello et al., 2001; Genetos et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this established observation.

claim: Calcium elevations and ATP release result in autocrine and paracrine purinergic receptor signaling.
source: Following mechanical stimulation of rodent and human osteoblasts, transient intracellular free calcium ([Ca2+]i) elevations and ATP release are among the earliest detectable events, which result in autocrine and paracrine purinergic (P2) receptor signaling (Robling and Turner, 2009; Romanello et al., 2001; Genetos et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this established mechanism.

claim: Vesicular release of lysosomes or secretory vesicles is a main mechanism of regulated ATP release in mammalian cells.
source: Vesicular release of lysosomes or secretory vesicles, or conductive release via channels such as Maxi anion channels, Volume-regulated anion channels (VRAC), Connexins or Pannexins are the main mechanisms of regulated ATP release in mammalian cells (Mikolajewicz et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this established mechanism.

claim: Conductive release via channels is a main mechanism of regulated ATP release in mammalian cells.
source: Vesicular release of lysosomes or secretory vesicles, or conductive release via channels such as Maxi anion channels, Volume-regulated anion channels (VRAC), Connexins or Pannexins are the main mechanisms of regulated ATP release in mammalian cells (Mikolajewicz et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this established mechanism.

claim: Pathological ATP spillage occurs from traumatically damaged cells.
source: Pathological ATP spillage also occurs from traumatically damaged cells (Burnstock and Verkhratskii, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this established observation.

claim: Non-lethal membrane injury has been demonstrated in vivo in several tissues under physiological conditions.
source: Of interest, non-lethal membrane injury has been demonstrated in vivo in several tissues (McNeil and Steinhardt, 2003), including bone (Yu et al., 2017), under physiological conditions.
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this established observation.

claim: Non-lethal membrane injury has been demonstrated in bone under physiological conditions.

claim: The mechanism of facilitated cell membrane repair involves Ca2+/PKC-dependent vesicular exocytosis.
source: The mechanism of facilitated cell membrane repair has been described and involves Ca2+/PKC-dependent vesicular exocytosis (Togo et al., 1999).

claim: Transient membrane disruption is required to induce global [Ca2+]i elevations in osteoblasts.
source: Since we have previously demonstrated that transient membrane disruption is required to induce global [Ca2+]i elevations in osteoblasts (Lopez-Ayon et al., 2014), we were particularly interested in understanding the contribution of membrane injury to mechanically induced ATP release.
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study by the authors to support this observation.

claim: Mechanical stimulation of C2-OB, CB-OB, and BM-OB induced qualitatively similar transient global [Ca2+]i elevations.
source: Osteoblasts from three different sources, C2-OB, CB-OB, and BM-OB, were loaded with [Ca2+]i dye Fura2 and mechanically stimulated with a glass micropipette, which induced qualitatively similar transient global [Ca2+]i elevations, consistent with prior work (Robling and Turner, 2009; Romanello et al., 2001; Genetos et al., 2005) (Figure 1A–C, Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental observations and references figures showing calcium responses in different osteoblast types.

claim: L-type VSCC inhibitor Nifedipine significantly reduced the amplitude of mechanically-stimulated [Ca2+]i transients.
source: L-type voltage-sensitive calcium channel (VSCC) inhibitor Nifedipine and P2 antagonist PPADS significantly reduced the amplitude of mechanically-stimulated [Ca2+]i transients (Figure 1D).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental findings with pharmacological inhibitors and references a figure.

claim: P2 antagonist PPADS significantly reduced the amplitude of mechanically-stimulated [Ca2+]i transients.
source: L-type voltage-sensitive calcium channel (VSCC) inhibitor Nifedipine and P2 antagonist PPADS significantly reduced the amplitude of mechanically-stimulated [Ca2+]i transients (Figure 1D).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental findings with pharmacological inhibitors and references a figure.

claim: L-type VSCC activation occurred gradually.
source: L-type VSCC activation occurred gradually (Figure 1E) while the P2 receptor-driven component of the response peaked within seconds of stimulation (Figure 1F).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental observations and references a figure.

claim: The P2 receptor-driven component of the response peaked within seconds of stimulation.
source: L-type VSCC activation occurred gradually (Figure 1E) while the P2 receptor-driven component of the response peaked within seconds of stimulation (Figure 1F).

claim: Shortly after a single osteoblast was mechanically stimulated, neighboring cells exhibited delayed secondary [Ca2+]i responses.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Robling and Turner, 2009; Romanello et al., 2001; Genetos et al., 2005), shortly after a single osteoblast was mechanically stimulated, neighboring cells exhibited delayed secondary [Ca2+]i responses (Figure 1G).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental observations consistent with cited literature and references a figure.

claim: P2 receptors mediated the secondary response in all three osteoblast models.
source: Pharmacological interventions revealed that P2 receptors mediated the secondary response in all three osteoblast models, while a tendency for GAP junction involvement was observed in BM-OB responses (Figure 1H).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental findings with pharmacological interventions and references a figure.

claim: ATP release occurred within seconds after mechanical stimulation.
source: Simultaneous recording of [ATP]e and [Ca2+]i demonstrated that ATP release occurred within seconds after mechanical stimulation (time to peak release: 1.64 ± 0.36 s) and preceded the onset of [Ca2+]i responses in neighboring cells (Figure 2).
